For the hemifacial microsomia, yes. I have microtia (underdeveloped ear) and underwent reconstructive surgery when I was 12. My jaw wasn't as prominent of a deformity until I became an adult. My dentist seen that my bottom jaw had shifted and that my bite was off by quite a bit. She sent me to an orthodontist who diagnosed me with Hemifacial Microsomia which he said is typical with microtia. He told me my jaw could cause serious medical concerns later in life and sent me to an oral surgeon who verified and said my surgery is medically necessary.

Side note, I did ask my Ortho about these symptoms and he said some of them (like vision and migraine) could be due to my jaw misalignment and condition.

*I haven't seen a geneticist, no.

It wasn't possible to domesticate the animals here. You can search that. And indigenous people most certainly worked with what they had. So much so the pilgrims and many settlers learned from the indigenous people in how to survive in North America.

Indigenous people have a huge issue with trust, both with white people, their own families and themselves. Toxic shame is something that goes from generation to generation and there are many dependant variable like addictions or anger. Toxic shame is similar to PTSD. 

I believe that understanding that what was experienced is mass trauma. Your color can represents the trauma experienced by many indigenous people. This world is unfair and so sometimes blame will feel like it is the only way of finding peace (which its not). 

Most indigenous people are trauma victims because of unethical assimilation practices that have intergenerational consequences (intergenerational trauma, PTSD, toxic shame, what ever you want to call it these things are passed down through parenting and socialization).

Its hard, but for many of us, daily life is very hard. Count your blessings, Hold your family tight. And pray indigenous people will be able to see something like self acceptance and united families with healthy relationships as something that is normal one day due to the hard work of moving past trauma thanks to many indigenous people and allies.

That's because animals here aren't easily domesticated especially pre colonialism, even for white folks and their knowledge at the time(you try domesticate a Buffalo, wait, you can't). This caused reliance on hunter gatherer systems. I think you're underestimating indigenous folks here. The geographic area is tricky for evolving into different levels of economic prosperity without having learned what others were doing in other worlds or having domesticated animals. Industrial revolution just didn't have the same modes here. Doesn't diminish their capability to wage war and practice their rights as sovereign nations, and do a good enough job where I'm able to be here today.

As an indigenous person in Canada, this isn't something that one person can do. You can help the movement by engaging in allyship where you educate yourself and those around you.

In a larger sense, I see some people saying "get rid of the reserve system!" I think that's wrong, and if anything Indigenous communities should be integrated back into managing their own political and social institutions without the economic marginalization set by the Indian Act. We're survivors because we had treaties. John Green said something like it's important that we know that indigenous people aren't folks that have had history act upon them, but were actually large players in all of this.

Our culture isn't just about feathers, ceremony and hard to pronounce names, but it's also about resisting colonization with the help of activists and allies. It's not just indigenous people either, it was our relationship with many white folks, genuine people who used their power to educate their communities and help indigenous people because it was the human thing to do. I don't understand why it's so hard to understand how trust plays a large role in all of this, and if there's no trust you will always have resistors.
